explanation: Emoji joins Japanese e, picture, and moji, written character. Its likeness to the English word 'emotion' is a coincidence, which is why so many people assume the two are related.

claims.text: The word 'emoji' comes from Japanese e (picture) and moji (written character).
The Japanese parts of 'emoji' do not mean emotion and icon, face and symbol, or feeling and sign.
The resemblance between 'emoji' and the English word 'emotion' is a coincidence; the two words are unrelated.

issues.note: Explanation: 'is a coincidence, which is why so many people assume the two are related' makes the coincidence the cause of the assumption, when it is the likeness that misleads. Something like 'is a coincidence, though it leads many people to assume...' reads better. No fact changes.

evidence.restatement: The Japanese elements are e and moji only, so none of the three rival glosses (feeling and sign, emotion and icon, face and symbol) is a translation of the word.
